**Requirements:**  
**Dictionary of specific terminology**

| Term | Definition |
| :---- | :---- |
| Chess Board | An 8 x 8 grid where the game will be played. The board will be displayed in a Tkinter window that is 900x700 pixels with a dark theme. |
| Chess Piece | Game pieces like a pawn, rook, knight, bishop, and etc. |
| Player | User playing the game. Opposing the AI Opponent. |
| AI Opponent | The algorithmic computer controlled opponent that will be the opposing user. |
| Legal Move | A move that follows the rules of chess. |
| Check | When the King is under the threat of being captured. |
| Checkmate | When the King has no legal move to escape and is under the threat of being captured. |
| Stalemate | When a player has no more legal moves, but their king is not currently in check, resulting in a draw. |
| Point Value | Point value assigned to each piece. For example, both the knight and bishop are worth 3 points. Where the queen is worth 9 points. |
| Point-Based AI | The AI opponent chooses moves by maximizing move value instead of using the generalized min-max algorithm. |
| Game Over | The condition where the game ends because of either a checkmate, stalemate, or a point-based win from either the AI opponent or player. Another instance of the game ending could be running out of time. |
| Timer | A count down from a specific time that will indicate when the game ends (winner will be based on who has the highest amount of points). |
| Position Value | The score given to a move based on how useful the destination square is.  |
| Development Value | The score given to a move that helps move pieces from their starting positions into more useful positions. For example, moving the knight to the centre to gain more control. |
| Safety Value | The score given to a move based on how safe the moved piece is after the move. A move has a lower safety value if it places an important piece where it can be captured. |
| Small Random Tie-Break Value | A small random score added to a move when multiple legal moves account to similar values. This is to prevent the AI from making the same moves each time. Value must be really small so that it does not deter it from its algorithmic behaviour. |
| Move Value | The total score assigned to a possible AI move. It is calculated by combining the point value, position value, development value, safety value, and a small random tie-break value. The AI will use the move value to determine the best legal move. |
| Random Promotion | The twist: At one random point in the game between moves 6 and 16 inclusive, a black AI pawn piece will be promoted into a stronger black piece. The pawn can transform into either a queen, rook, bishop, or knight. |
| Bias Value | A value that is derived from the predicted player’s move value after the chosen AI move. This value can only be subtracted from the total move value as a way to prevent risky moves. |

**User Standpoint Description**

For the user playing against the AI opponent, the software must provide the following:

**Game Setup**

* The game launches and displays a chess board.  
* All chess pieces will be in their starting positions.  
* The player will be allotted the bottom half of the board.  
* The AI will control the opposite side of the board.  
* The player always plays as White with Black pieces at the top and White pieces at the bottom.  
* A timer will be displayed and will begin counting down after the player clicks “start game”.  
* Both the player and AI will have their own timers.  
* The user can see all the chess board, chess pieces and their placement, current score, and the time remaining.

**Gameplay**

* The player can see the chess board, chess pieces and their placement, current score, captured pieces, career statistics, and the time remaining in the side panel.  
* The player must type out the position of the piece they are trying to move and also write out the destination square. For example, moving a pawn from A2 (initial position) to A3 (final position) would be A2A3 or a2a3. The move is entered in the side panel text field and submitted by pressing the "Move" button.  
* The engine will verify whether it is legal or not  
  * If the move is illegal the move will not be allowed and the canvas will not update and will remain in its initial position.  
  * If the move is legal then the canvas will update to the player's move.  
* After the player makes a legal move the AI opponent will take its turn.  
* The AI opponent chooses a move by scoring possible legal moves using point values, position value, development value, and safety value.  
* At the beginning of the game, the AI checks the stored opening patterns in order and plays the first opening move sequence that matches the current move history.  
* If the current opening pattern cannot be used because of the player’s moves, the AI will switch to its general point-based move system.  
* The AI will generate all possible legal moves for its own pieces.  
* Each possible move will receive a move value based on the point value, position value, development value, safety value, and a small random tie-break value.  
* The AI will determine the player’s possible moves after each possible AI move and use the same move value system to attach values. Based on each possibility, the AI will subtract a bias value from risky moves to lower the move value to prevent playing risky moves.  
* The move with the highest move value will be played by the AI.  
* After the AI’s move, the canvas will update and it will once again be the player's turn.  
* If a piece is captured, the captured piece will be removed from the board.  
  * The point value assigned to the piece will be allotted to either the player or AI depending on who captured the piece.  
* The game will continue until checkmate, stalemate, the timer running out, or either the player or AI reach the target score.

**Detailed Requirements:**

The following is a flowchart of how the point-based move system works:

\\

**Move Value Calculation:**

The point value works by determining all the possible legal moves and determining all possible captures. When multiple pieces are on the multiple capture list, the piece attacked is the one with the highest points. For example, if a knight has the ability to take a pawn or a queen, it will take the queen. A pawn is worth 1 point and a queen is worth 9 points. The next move with the highest point value will be the one that will have a higher point value compared to the other move. The numeric value of the point value is determined by the worth of a piece. For example, if the queen can be taken, when calculating the move value, a value of 9 will be used for the point value.

The development value is applied only to pieces that have not yet moved from their starting position. The numerical value of the development value is based on how many squares the piece gains control over (mobility). For example, moving the knights and bishops near the centre of the board allows them to control the most squares, allotting them the maximum development value. The more squares a piece can control, the more development value it incurs. This is only applicable to early games where pieces have not moved from their starting position. After a piece moves, it loses the ability to have a development value, instead the position value takes over. Every piece gets a development value. The square control value is determined by calculating all the legal moves of the current piece to determine the possible options, then calculating all the possible legal moves of the possible options to determine how many squares it can control. The numerical range for the development value ranges between 0 to 27\. The reason why it is up to 27 is because the queen can control 27 squares. Something to keep in mind is that a home piece (same colour piece) occupying a square is not a legal placement for a piece. The development value of each possible move is saved so that it can be used when calculating move value. 

The position value is a subsequent process of the development value. The way the position value works is by essentially doing the same thing for development value, but after the piece has moved. Unlike the development value which counts total squares controlled, position value measures how many of those squares contain enemy pieces that can be captured. This represents a piece’s active threat level. For example, a knight might be able to move to two spots. One spot might allow it to control 5 squares but also attack 3 enemy pieces. Another spot might let it control 5 squares but attack no pieces. The first option would be better. The position value also differentiates itself from the development value by determining if the next move is threatened by an enemy piece. If the square is threatened, a value of 1 will be deducted from the position value. If the same square is protected by an ally piece, a value of 1 will be added to the position value. The position value ranges from \-8 to 16\. The minimum of \-8 occurs when a piece can only move to a square where all the squares are threatened by enemy pieces and are not protected. The maximum of 16 occurs when a piece threatens many enemy pieces (up to 8\) on squares that are all protected by friendly pieces (to be clear this is like the next move of the AI and is not referring to the enemy squares being protected by friendly pieces that does not make sense). The position value is calculated using three components after a piece moves to its destination, this consists of the following:

1. Enemy pieces threatened (0 to 8): From the new position, all legal moves should be calculated and as a subsequent process, the threats that can be given to the opponent should be counted. Each capturable enemy piece adds \+1 to the position value.  
2. Protected square adjustment (0 to 8): From the new position, for all possible legal moves from that position, check if that square is protected by a friendly piece. Each ally piece that protects the end move will add \+1 to the position value.  
3. Threatened square adjustment (0 to \-8): From the new position, for all possible legal moves from that position, check if that square is threatened by an enemy piece. Each threatening enemy piece subtracts \-1 from the position value.

Therefore, the final formula for the position value is position value \= (enemy pieces threatened) \+ (protected squares) \- (threatening pieces).

	The safety value can be described by determining the liability of each move. When a piece is moved, as the position value earlier had determined the safety of the next move, the safety value determines what is left open once the move is completed. The way safety value is calculated is by determining what pieces remain vulnerable to attack from moving a piece. When a piece moves from its starting square, it may have been protecting friendly pieces from being attacked by enemy pieces at that location. After the move, these pieces are left vulnerable to enemy attack. The safety value only penalizes moves where the pieces left vulnerable are worth more than the piece that was initially moved. For example, if a knight that is worth 3 points is placed in front of a rook that is worth 5 points, and the knight is moved, it leaves the rook vulnerable to attack assuming in this case that there is another rook or enemy piece that can occupy that square the next move. Since the rook is worth more, the safety value for moving the knight would be a negative value. However, if the vulnerable piece is still protected by an ally piece, the safety value is neutralized since the piece is no longer vulnerable. Every piece gets a safety value. A piece is considered vulnerable if enemy pieces can legally occupy the square the ally piece is on. The protection value used to determine whether or not the safety value can be neutralized is determined by calculating all possible legal moves of the ally pieces that can occupy the vulnerable pieces position on the board. If it can be protected, the move is considered safe. The safety value ranges from 0 to 8\. The maximum penalty of 8 occurs when moving a pawn that has a value of 1 which exposes a queen that is worth 9 points to a threat by the opponent (9-1=8). The minimum of 0 occurs when no valuable pieces are exposed, or when the pieces are protected by ally pieces. The formula for safety value is vulnerable piece \- moving piece value, where if the vulnerable piece is protected by an ally square the calculation is skipped and the value for safety value is simply 0\.

Random Tie Breaking Value is determined by using the random library to choose a number between 1-20, where the numbers 1-10 correspond to \- 0.10 to \- 0.01 and the numbers 11-20 correspond to 0.01 to 0.1, with both moving either up or down in intervals of 0.01. The addition of the random tie breaking value ensures that no move gets a tiebreak value of 0.00, and where there is a 50% chance of positive or negative adjustment.

	The move value is determined by the cumulative sum through all the values listed above. Negative values occur when a move exposes valuable pieces, incurring a high safety penalty with no capture or position advantage. Positive values indicate strong moves with captures, development, gain in positional advantage or possible threats. The formula is move value \= point value \+ (development value or position value) \- safety value \+ random tiebreaking value. For the AI, all possible legal moves are determined, then the move value is determined for every move and the move with the highest move value is chosen.

	The bias value is determined by essentially  repeating the process, but for the enemy/player. The point value, development value, position value, safety value, and random tie breaking value is used to determine the move value for all possible player legal moves. The bias value represents how much the player can threaten the AI after the AI makes a move. To calculate this, the AI simulates all possible legal responses from the enemy player, determining the player’s best counter moves for each possible AI move. After simulating all possible moves by the player after each possible AI move, each player counter move has its move value calculated which I will refer to as enemy move value. The enemy move value utilizes the same formula for move value as the AI. The highest enemy move value represents the threat level. The bias value is based on the following three factors:

1. If the enemy move value is \<= 3, the bias value is zero.  
2. If the enemy move value is \> 3 and  \<= 5, the bias is the enemy move value \* 0.3  
3. If the enemy move value is \> 5, the bias is enemy move value \* 0.5

This bias value is then subtracted from the AI move value to penalize AI moves that are risky, forcing the AI to make moves in places where player response is weak.

**Bias Value Enemy Possible Legal Move Simulation**

The bias value is determined by simulating all possible legal moves of the player in response to all possible legal moves of the AI. The bias value is then subtracted from the AI’s own move value, acting as a penalty to risky moves. The following are the steps that are used to simulate all the possible legal moves:

1. The AI generates all its possible legal moves on the current board. For each individual AI move, it is simulated on a copied board. This makes it so that the AI can play its legal move on the copied board rather than changing the actual board. This means that if the AI has 20 possible legal moves, each move is simulated on its own copied board where each board represents the state of the game after that move has been played. Once the simulated move is complete, the system generates all possible legal moves that can be played by the player, effectively simulating all the possible legal responses that can be played for the AI legal move. The reasoning behind multiple simulated boards per legal AI move is that the player's legal responses for every AI move will differ.   
2. Each of the player’s possible legal moves is evaluated by using the same point value, development value, position value, and safety value structure that is used to calculate the move value for the AI. By using the same formula, the system ensures that the player’s threat level is measured on the same scale as the AI’s own move value calculation (same method). However, the random tie break value is not used during the simulated player response calculations so that the bias result stays consistent. After all possible legal player responses have been evaluated for that specific copied board, the highest move among them is identified. This value represents the player’s best counter move to the AI’s move and is the move that is chosen for the enemy move value.  
3. This process is repeated sequentially for every possible AI legal move. As mentioned earlier, each move produces its own copied board, and its own set of possible player response moves. After all AI moves have been simulated and all enemy move values have been determined, the bias value is calculated from the threat level of the best player response for each simulated AI move. As mentioned in the earlier detailed explanation of the bias value, it follows the same methodology. The calculated bias value is then subtracted from the AI’s original move value to produce the final move values for all possible legal AI moves, ultimately leading to the move that is chosen.

**User Interface Mockup:**

The following is a description of the chess.com-style GUI. The window is 900x700 pixels with a dark theme and non-resizable.

**Start Screen Layout:**

The user is presented with a dark background (#302E2B). On the left is an 8x8 chess board with all pieces in their starting positions. The board uses green (#769656) and beige (#EEEED2) squares that are 70 pixels each. A side panel on the right (250px wide, #262421 background) contains all the controls.

A timer sits above the board showing "Black 10:00" and another timer below the board showing "White 10:00". The active player's timer is displayed in white text while the inactive timer uses muted text.

The side panel contains:
* The title "Move Value Chess" at the top
* A "You are playing as White" label indicating the player's colour
* An "AI Target Score" entry field (defaults to 10) that sets how many points the AI needs to win
* A green [Start Game] button to begin

**Main Game Screen Layout:**

After pressing [Start Game], the side panel updates to show:
* A "Your Turn" or "AI Thinking..." label indicating who is currently playing
* The current score: "Player: X pts | AI: Y pts | Target: Z"
* Captures for both sides showing which pieces have been taken
* A "Lifetime: W: X L: Y D: Z" label showing career stats
* Status messages such as "Your move" or "Invalid format! Use E2E4"
* A move entry field where the player types moves in algebraic notation (e.g. E2E4)
* A green [Move] button to submit the move
* A [New Game] button to restart

The board updates after each move. The player's timer runs down during their turn and the AI's timer runs down during the AI's turn. When one timer reaches zero, the game ends and the player with the most points wins.

**Game Over Screen:**

When the game ends, a dark overlay (#1A1A1A) appears over the board area showing:
* "Game Over" in large bold text
* The result: "You Win!" in green, "You Lose!" in red, or "Draw!" in yellow
* The reason for the game ending, such as "Checkmate!" or "Time's up!"
* The final scores
* Lifetime statistics
* A green [Exit] button to close the window

The side panel widgets are hidden during the game over screen. Timers remain visible showing the final time.

The AI should choose the move with the highest final move value and prevent itself from being captured the next turn. |

| 04 | Check Response Test | When the AI is under check by the player, the AI should only be able to either block the threat, or move the king to safety. |

**Implementation:**

The final program was implemented using Tkinter and python. The program is separated into multiple files primarily because of the distinct code pieces that are better suited to be separated into multiple files where their functions can be imported rather than have all the code in one massive file. The game can be run from main.py, which opens a Tkinter window and ties in all the other files.  
The program uses data.py to store the starting board, piece symbols, position values (each distinct piece has its own placement and value allotted to it on every square on the board). Each piece's movement and rules that apply to them with regard to capturing opponent pieces are handled and programmed in the move\_rules.py file. As mentioned before, the bias evaluation system creates a copied board to simulate moves, to tackle this, in the board\_logic.py file we have handles the following: copying the board, generating legal moves, checking check, checkmate, and stalemate. The AI move calculations are handled in ai\_engine.py. To help the AI start the game effectively, we have hardcoded a couple of common chess openings in bookmoves.py that are chosen based on the player's opening move and can be diverged from in case of a threat. The changing match information, scores, captures, move history, random promotion turn, player/AI colour, and saved history are handled by game\_state.py.

The GUI in main.py was redesigned to look like a chess.com-style interface. The window size was changed from 700x700 to 900x700 with a dark background (#302E2B) and made non-resizable. The board squares were enlarged from 60px to 70px and recoloured using green (#769656) and beige (#EEEED2) instead of grey and white. A dark side panel (250px wide, #262421) was added on the right side of the window to hold all controls and information. Timers were placed above and below the board, showing "Black" and "White" with the remaining time. The active player's timer is highlighted in white while the inactive timer uses muted text. The player always plays as White and the side panel shows "You are playing as White". Button styling follows a flat green theme for action buttons and grey for secondary buttons. The game over screen now uses a dark overlay (#1A1A1A) over the board area instead of the previous yellow box, keeping the board visible in the background.

Right below is an explanation of how chess\_lifetime.txt and chess\_history.txt are utilized to store various game data that extends beyond the live game.

**Design Documents:**  
**Database and Data Structure**

The program uses two text files to store the game history across multiple sessions to track progress and see the exact moves that were played. Chess\_history.txt contains data for the date and time of the match, result, player’s capture score, AI’s capture score, player’s remaining time, and the AI’s remaining time. Chess\_lifetime.txt stores all the matches won, lost, and drawn and can be seen in the GUI directly. During the game, the board, scores, captures, move history, opening moves, and piece values are stored and manipulated using both 2D lists and dictionaries.

| File Name | Description |
| :---- | :---- |
| main.py | This runs the main game window and creates the Tkinter interface, handles user inputs, updates the board, controls timers, and connects the rest of the project together. The GUI includes a dark-themed chess.com-style layout with a side panel for controls and colour selection, timers above and below the board, and a game over overlay. |
| move\_rules.py | This file consists of all the legal moves of all the different pieces in chess. This file is also responsible for determining what types of capture each piece can have. For example, the pawn captures only diagonally. This also contains helper functions that help validate moves. |
| board\_logic.py | This file contains all the board level logic like copying the board over to simulate moves for the AI. |
| ai\_engine.py | This file contains the bulk of the calculations that are responsible for the move value.  |
| game\_state.py | This file stores the changing match information like the scores, captures from either side, move history, current player/AI colour, and target score (that would have been initially set). |
| data.py | This file stores the starting chessboard and the initial positions of all the pieces. It also contains all the position values of all the chess pieces dependent on their position on the board.  |
| bookmoves.py | This file stores hardcoded opening patterns and allows the AI to begin the game strong with common opening patterns. |
| chess\_history.txt | This text file stores the match history records. It logs every chess game played between the player and the AI. The records for each match contains the date and time of the match, result, player’s capture score, AI’s capture score, player’s remaining time, AI’s remaining time. |
| chess\_lifetime.txt | This text file stores all the matches won, lost, and drawn. |
